reference.source: DeLee, Drez & Miller's Orthopaedic Sports Medicine
clinicalPearls: Lateral patellar dislocation is by far the usual direction, typically caused by a twisting valgus force on a flexed knee or a direct medial blow.
A first-time dislocation often reduces spontaneously as the knee extends, and a tense haemarthrosis is common.
The medial patellofemoral ligament is the primary passive restraint to lateral translation and is almost invariably torn in first dislocation.
Key anatomical risk factors are trochlear dysplasia, patella alta, an increased tibial tubercle to trochlear groove distance, and rotational malalignment or ligamentous laxity.
A positive apprehension test and a J-sign on active extension support the diagnosis of maltracking and instability.
Always exclude an osteochondral fracture of the medial patellar facet or lateral femoral condyle after dislocation.
First-time dislocation without a loose body is usually treated conservatively with bracing and physiotherapy targeting the vastus medialis obliquus and hip.
Recurrent instability may require medial patellofemoral ligament reconstruction, with bony procedures such as tibial tubercle osteotomy or trochleoplasty for underlying dysplasia.
reference.pathophysiology: Patellar stability depends on the interplay of static restraints (the medial patellofemoral ligament, trochlear geometry and patellar shape), dynamic restraints (the quadriceps, especially the vastus medialis obliquus) and overall limb alignment. Lateral dislocation occurs when a valgus and external rotation force acts on a flexed, weight-bearing knee, overcoming the medial soft tissues and tearing the medial patellofemoral ligament from its femoral or patellar attachment. Predisposing morphology - trochlear dysplasia with a shallow or convex trochlea, patella alta with late trochlear engagement, a laterally positioned tibial tubercle, rotational malalignment and generalised laxity - lowers the force threshold for displacement and drives recurrence. Each event risks osteochondral shear injury and progressive patellofemoral chondral wear.
additionalDifferentials: Anterior cruciate ligament rupture, which also causes acute haemarthrosis after a twisting injury
Isolated osteochondral fracture without persistent instability
Patellofemoral pain syndrome or chondromalacia patellae
Referred hip pathology such as a slipped capital femoral epiphysis in adolescents
additionalInvestigations: Radiographs including skyline/Merchant views for patellar tilt, subluxation and osteochondral fragments
MRI to assess the site of medial patellofemoral ligament tear, chondral injury and the characteristic bone bruise pattern
CT or MRI measurement of the tibial tubercle to trochlear groove distance and grading of trochlear dysplasia
Assessment of patella alta using the Insall-Salvati or Caton-Deschamps index
Rotational profile assessment of femoral anteversion and tibial torsion
Beighton score to assess generalised ligamentous laxity
redFlags: A locked knee or mechanical block suggesting a displaced osteochondral fragment or loose body
An irreducible dislocation or gross deformity
Neurovascular compromise following a high-energy injury
A tense haemarthrosis with fat globules indicating an osteochondral fracture
Medial or multidirectional dislocation suggesting an iatrogenic cause or connective tissue disorder
reference.prognosis: Many first-time dislocators do well with conservative treatment, but recurrence is common in young patients with dysplastic anatomy. Surgical stabilisation, particularly ligament reconstruction combined with correction of bony risk factors, has a high success rate in reducing redislocation.
pitfalls: Missing an osteochondral fracture on initial radiographs after the patella has relocated.
Attributing the haemarthrosis solely to an anterior cruciate ligament injury and overlooking patellar dislocation.
Reconstructing the medial patellofemoral ligament without addressing underlying bony malalignment, leading to failure.
Overtightening a ligament graft, causing medial overload and stiffness.
Neglecting hip and core weakness during rehabilitation.
references: DeLee, Drez & Miller's Orthopaedic Sports Medicine
Apley's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
management: Reduce an acute lateral dislocation by knee extension and then protect the knee in a brace with progressive mobilisation
Prioritise rehabilitation for first episodes, strengthening the quadriceps and vastus medialis obliquus, hip abductors, and external rotators, with patellar bracing or taping to improve tracking
Fix or excise osteochondral fractures of the medial patellar facet or lateral femoral condyle after dislocation
Offer medial patellofemoral ligament reconstruction for recurrent instability, addressing bony abnormalities with trochleoplasty or tibial-tubercle transfer when they drive redislocation
Define anatomical risk factors such as trochlear dysplasia, patella alta, tibial-tubercle-to-trochlear-groove distance, rotational malalignment, and laxity to plan intervention
Manage jointly with orthopaedics and physiotherapy, tailoring surgery to the individual's anatomy
